nodes.description: Antibodies against growth hormone appearing after exogenous GH is started. Titre and binding capacity matter more than presence: high-titre antibodies produce secondary growth arrest, while low-binding-capacity antibodies have been observed alongside sustained catch-up growth for at least three years.

evidence.snippet: Individuals with IGHD 1A develop severe dwarfism in early infancy and often develop anti-GH antibodies after receiving exogenous GH.
She was treated with biosynthetic GH resulting in long-lasting catch-up growth during at least three years, despite a clinically irrelevant appearance of low binding capacity GH antibodies.

nodes.description:
The rate-limiting state, and the one from which both arms of this entry follow. It is what separates type IA from the other Mendelian forms: types IB, II and III all have diminished GH, type IA has none.
Curating absence rather than deficiency as the central node is deliberate. A quantity that is reduced and a quantity that is zero behave differently in the immune system, and the difference is what the tolerance arm below depends on.
nodes.id: Complete Absence of Endogenous Growth Hormone

evidence.snippet: At least four Mendelian types of isolated GH deficiency (IGHD) have been delineated based on the mode of inheritance and the degree of GH deficiency: IGHD type IA, autosomal recessive with absent endogenous GH; type IB, autosomal recessive with diminished GH; type II, autosomal dominant with diminished GH; and type III, X-linked with diminished GH.

nodes.description: Bone age lags behind chronological age, as in growth hormone deficiency generally. Not specific to type IA.

evidence.snippet: Although short stature, delayed growth velocity, and delayed skeletal maturation all occur with IGHD, none are specific for IGHD 1A.

nodes.description:
The arm that makes this disease distinctive. Because no growth hormone was ever present, the immune system never encountered it as self, and recombinant GH given therapeutically is seen as a foreign protein. Many patients develop anti-GH antibodies, and those antibodies can prevent the growth response the treatment was given to produce.
The evidence that this is a tolerance failure rather than an idiosyncratic drug reaction is the carrier state. Heterozygotes with one deleted allele and one allele producing non-truncated protein have circulating GH and are usually immune tolerant - tolerance follows the presence of endogenous hormone, not the genotype. That is as close to a controlled comparison as a rare disease offers.
nodes.id: Failure of Immune Tolerance to Growth Hormone

evidence.snippet: Individuals with IGHD 1A develop severe dwarfism in early infancy and often develop anti-GH antibodies after receiving exogenous GH.
These antibodies can prevent the growth response expected from exogenous GH therapy.
Individuals who are heterozygous for a GH1 gene deletion but whose other GH1 allele is not deleted and produces a non truncated product are usually immune tolerant.

nodes.description:
GH1 lies on chromosome 17 and is expressed in the somatotrophs of the anterior pituitary. Type IA is defined by lesions that abolish bioactive GH entirely: deletions ranging from about 6.7 kb to 45 kb, and also frameshift and nonsense mutations.
The definitional point matters for diagnosis. The entity is complete GH deficiency caused by severe loss-of-function at GH1, not "the deletion syndrome" - a patient with a homozygous nonsense mutation and no deletion has type IA, and a deletion-only definition would miss them.
The deletions have an unusual origin: they recur through unequal meiotic recombination rather than descending from a common ancestral allele, so the same deletion appearing in unrelated families is not evidence of shared ancestry.

evidence.snippet: GH1 gene deletions, frameshifts, or nonsense mutations cause complete absence of GH in IGHD 1A.
Thus IGHD 1A is best described as being complete GHD caused by severe loss of function GH1 gene mutations rather than being limited to only those having GH1 gene deletions.
Interestingly, GH1 gene deletions are recurring mutations that can arise through unequal recombination in meiosis rather than by allele sharing through common descent.
Most patients with IGHD type IA have heterogeneous deletions, ranging in size from 6.7 kb to 45 kb, that encompass the entire gene encoding for pituitary GH, GH-1.

nodes.description: Infantile hypoglycaemia, reflecting the loss of growth hormone's counter-regulatory role. It can precede recognisable growth failure and is one of the few features that brings these infants to attention before six months.

evidence.snippet: While affected individuals can have short lengths at birth and hypoglycemia in infancy, all develop severe dwarfism by six months of age.

nodes.description: Without ligand there is no growth hormone receptor signalling and no downstream generation of the growth-promoting response. Clinically this is unremarkable in the newborn period - length at birth may be short but need not be - and then declares itself decisively, with all affected individuals reaching severe dwarfism by six months.

nodes.description:
Hormone replacement is the treatment, and in this disorder it is also the exposure that creates the second problem. Replacement produces catch-up growth where antibodies do not neutralise it; where they do, growth arrests secondarily.
The Italian family in the cited series shows the range within a single genotype: three siblings with the same 45-kb deletion, two developing high-titre antibodies with secondary growth arrest, and the third growing normally with only very low-titre antibodies.

evidence.snippet: Two of the affected children developed high-titer anti-hGH antibodies after recombinant hGH treatment with secondary growth arrest, whereas the third one maintained normal growth in the presence of very low-titer antibodies.
These antibodies can prevent the growth response expected from exogenous GH therapy.

nodes.description:
The rescue option when replacement has been neutralised, and the one that completes the entry's argument: if anti-GH antibodies block the hormone from reaching its receptor, giving the mediator downstream of that receptor bypasses the block entirely. IGF-1 is not growth hormone, so the antibodies do not see it.
Curated as second-line with a heterogeneous response rather than as a mainstay, because the three cited reports disagree with each other in an instructive way. The 1993 case had anti-GH titres reaching 1:1,000,000 and grew well for a year on IGF-I with no anti-IGF-I antibody formation. Two Brazilian children with 6.7-kb deletions achieved catch-up growth, at 6.7 to 8.4 cm/yr. A 2006 series of four patients called the growth response to rhIGF-I *moderate* and the overall outcome heterogeneous, with pubertal development and bone-age acceleration in the two treated at pubertal age.
So it works, it is not equivalent to effective GH replacement, and the age at which it is started appears to matter. The entry does not claim more than that.
One mechanistic detail from the Brazilian report is worth keeping: IGFBP-3 levels were low and did not rise on IGF-I, which the authors read as showing that the GH effect on IGFBP-3 is not IGF-I-mediated. That is a limit on how completely this treatment substitutes for the missing hormone - it replaces the growth-promoting arm, not everything growth hormone does.

evidence.snippet: Administration of IGF-I to IGHD type IA with poor response to GH therapy appears to have a beneficial effect on growth.
During IGF-I therapy he showed good linear growth without any side effects, such as hypoglycemia and anti-IGF-I antibody formation.
IGF-I therapy with increasing doses resulted in catch-up growth without side-effects.
Growth response during rhIGF-I treatment carried out in three of the patients was moderate, but pubertal development and bone age acceleration occurred in the two patients treated at pubertal age.
GH resistance, either caused by GH-Ab or GH receptor mutations, is still difficult to treat and results in a heterogeneous outcome.
IGFBP-3 levels were low (0.55 and 0.40 mg/I) and did not increase after IGF-I treatment, suggesting that this GH effect is not mediated by IGF-I
